<item>
<title>
<![CDATA[ Practical Guide to Hosting a Webex Integration on AWS ]]>
...
</title>
<description>
<![CDATA[ <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt6b347c282c632795/65e20f4137599906f470c73b/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-1.png?width=900&height=317&fit=crop" alt="Practical Guide to Hosting a Webex Integration on AWS" /> <p>The goal of this article is to go through the process of deploying a Webex integration on the AWS public cloud. The integration is built with Python and helps schedule Webex Webinars based on the information in a Smartsheet. It ties together three services via their respective APIs: Smartsheet, Webex Webinars, and Webex bot. Although not overly complex, this example isn’t trivial either. There are multiple technicalities in the deployment process that won’t be exposed in a simplest sample Webex bot project. While being mostly used for the Cisco Networking Academy Instructor Professional Development program, this integration is highly reusable, and the code is available on GitHub: *<a href='https://github.com/zhenyamorozov/smartsheet-webex' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>https://github.com/zhenyamorozov/smartsheet-webex</a></p> <p>When you build a Webex integration, no matter if you write code yourself or use a project from <a href='https://developer.cisco.com/codeexchange/' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Cisco Code Exchange</a>, after configuring and testing it locally, you eventually come to the need to host it in a cloud. When it runs in a cloud, there is no need to keep your computer always on for Webex bot to respond to commands and for automation to do its magic. There are multiple public cloud vendors, but in this example, I will use AWS. In AWS, we have several options to deploy a Python-based web application:</p> <ul> <li><strong>EC2 instance</strong> - you simply get a Linux virtual machine and run it as a web server for the application.</li> <li><strong>Containers</strong> - use AWS container services, such as ECS, EKS, or Fargate.</li> <li><strong>Lambda + API Gateway</strong> - a popular serverless microservice-oriented solution.</li> </ul> <p>Both container-based and serverless deployments require the application code to be adapted for these deployments to a certain degree. And because I wanted to keep the code as reusable as possible, the best choice is to deploy it in <strong>EC2</strong> - Elastic Compute Cloud.</p> <p>Running a web application on EC2 is like simply spinning up a virtual machine in the cloud and copying the application there. However, if we do this the straightforward way, we will have to worry about several things: launching the server, configuring the OS, setting up an environment for our application, and monitoring both the machine and the environment. Also, we would have to manage the code deployment process manually – whenever we make a change to the code, we must zip it and upload it to the VM or push it via SSH. Fortunately, there are AWS services that will let us simplify the deployment and maintenance of our app and cloud environment. In this case, I found <a href='https://aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Elastic Beanstalk</a> and <a href='https://aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Code Pipeline</a> to be particularly useful. </p> <p>We will use Elastic Beanstalk to spin up an EC2 instance and configure the cloud application environment, including permissions and environment variables.</p> <p>We will set up Code Pipeline to watch the GitHub repository of the project, and whenever a change is committed, automatically deploy the updated version of the code into the environment.</p> <p>So, let’s get started.</p> <h6>Creating a basic environment with Elastic Beanstalk</h6><p>Elastic Beanstalk, as the name suggests, is our shortcut to bring the application to the cloud. We create an environment for our application, and Beanstalk will manage the underlying infrastructure for us. So, we should not worry about OS management and maintenance. For example, if something breaks down in the EC2 instance, Elastic Beanstalk will kill it and spin up a fresh one instead.</p> <ol> <li>Log in to AWS Console and find the Elastic Beanstalk service. From the Elastic Beanstalk home page, click <strong>Create Environment</strong> and fill in the basic environment information on the Step 1 page:<ul> <li><strong>Environment tier</strong> – Web server environment. We are going to run a web server that will be serving incoming web requests relatively fast. The other option here is Worker, which is more suitable for long-running batch processing. Although the actual Webex webinar scheduling process may take up to 10 minutes (in cases of many sessions with considerable amounts of registrants), I saw no issues running it in a Web server environment.</li> <li><strong>Application name</strong> – any name for our application. Beanstalk will additionally create an application entity for us while creating the environment. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt7c5670f23d747046/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-2.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li><strong>Environment name</strong> will be populated automatically. No need to change this.</li> <li><strong>Domain</strong> – it is fine to use the random autogenerated domain name, but we can also customize it. It is a subdomain under the Elastic Beanstalk domain which does not cost anything extra and is perfectly usable in this case, as we won’t expose it to humans. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltbc63606e14420951/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-3.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li><strong>Platform</strong> – identifies which platform (OS and programming language/interpreter) we need. This project is written in Python, so the latest version of Python 3 and the recommended Linux OS should work. <em>Note: there is a <a href='https://github.com/WebexCommunity/WebexPythonSDK/issues/200' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>compatibility issue</a> with Python 3.12+ in Webex Python SDK, so until it is fixed, use Python 3.11 environment.</em></li> <li><strong>Application code</strong> – for now, let’s select Sample application. Later, we will set up Code Pipeline to deploy our code automatically. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltdfd19ca92f12b765/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-4.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li><strong>Presets</strong> – as this application is not supposed to serve a huge amount of internet users and does not require extra reliability, the <strong>Single instance</strong> option will be fine. It even runs free for some time if your AWS account is new, according to the AWS Free Tier policy. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltc3d0571ae298df43/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-5.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> </ul> </li> <li>On the next screen, the <strong>Service access</strong> is configured. Access between different services in the AWS cloud is controlled with roles. Elastic Beanstalk will assume the <strong>service role</strong> when accessing your EC2 instance. From the EC2 side, we need to create another role – the <strong>instance profile</strong> that will grant access to Elastic Beanstalk. This combination of roles will allow Elastic Beanstalk to do things like spin up, configure, monitor, and terminate instances. </li> <li>Select <strong>Create and use a new service role</strong>.</li> <li>To create an instance profile, open the AWS console in a new tab and navigate to <strong>IAM (Identity and Access Management service) – Roles</strong>. Click <strong>Create role</strong>, under <strong>Trusted entity type</strong>, select <strong>AWS service</strong>. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltc9f71dbe232971e7/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-6.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>For the <strong>Use case</strong>, choose <strong>EC2</strong>. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blte37ce9101317c3f1/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-7.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>On the next screen, search for and add the <code>AWSElasticBeanstalkWebTier</code> <strong>permission policy</strong>. This policy is managed by AWS and includes everything we need for now. We attach the permission policy to the role, and the role is attached to the EC2 service via an instance profile. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltc2962fac97cdf768/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-8.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Finally, name, review, and save the role. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltb673ca202f3ac970/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-9.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."> Return to the original tab, refresh the list of instance profiles, and select the one newly created. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt095a96352446d0c6/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-10.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."> Optionally, you can create an <strong>EC2 key pair</strong> to be able to log in to your EC2 instance via SSH. To create a key pair, open the AWS console in a new tab, navigate to EC2 – Network &amp; Security – Key Pairs, create it, and save the keys.</li> <li>In Step 3 we can select the default <strong>VPC</strong>. VPC is like a private network (VLAN) where the server will live.</li> <li>One thing we will certainly need is a <strong>Public IP address</strong>. When new messages are sent to the bot, the Webex service sends webhooks (HTTP requests) over the public internet. Our application needs to be able to receive them on this IP address. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt35161dfc69adc656/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-11.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."> <em>Please, note that since February 2024, AWS charges a fee for public IPv4 addresses.</em> The rest of this page may be left as default as our app is stateless and does not use any database.</li> <li>Step 4 is all about the instance configuration. No need to change it, but just note the <strong>IMDS service</strong> settings. IMDS (Instance Metadata Service) lets code running on the instance query basic information about the environment, such as public domain name. It is used by the Webex-Smartsheet application. IMDSv2 requires an additional authentication step which is implemented in the <a href='https://github.com/zhenyamorozov/smartsheet-webex/blob/0b45ca92165c7ca82a854592905af5104ff16c93/web.py#L51C48-L51C48' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>code</a>.<ul> <li><strong>EC2 security groups</strong> control network access between different hosts in the network (“data plane”). It is a smaller level of segmentation than VPC. In this case, we will place the EC2 instance in the default SG. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltebcf258f32858daa/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-12.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li><strong>Auto scaling group</strong> can manage a fleet of instances (virtual servers) to serve large high-load applications. In our case the load is small, so we’ll select <strong>Single instance</strong>. The scaling group will make sure the sole instance is running and healthy, and in case of any issues will terminate it and spin up a new one. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltb61134860722f9b4/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-13.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li><strong>Instance type</strong> is important, as it affects the cost of the running service. The smallest possible instance will be sufficient in our case – <strong>t3.nano</strong> at the moment. It should be also among the cheapest. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltb7e654e01be54c94/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-14.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> </ul> </li> <li>Let’s keep the rest of the settings default. We will get back to some of them later when we need to make changes. On the <strong>Review</strong> page, you can verify the configuration and finally click <strong>Submit</strong>. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt9e53dfbc54254b87/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-15.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> </ol> <p>After several minutes, the environment <strong>Health status</strong> should change to Ok, and on the <strong>Health</strong> tab, we should see the EC2 instance up and running.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltd58c5092d04c0684/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-16.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <p>If you click this environment’s domain name, the sample application will open in a new tab. This shows our environment is up, publicly accessible, and ready. In the next step, we will set up Code Pipeline to deploy our actual application code.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltc5255241acd81c82/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-17.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <h6>Setting up Code Pipeline</h6><p>With Code Pipeline, we will set up a simple CI/CD process. This service will monitor a repository in GitHub, and whenever a new commit is pushed, it will deploy the updated version of the application into our Elastic Beanstalk environment.</p> <ol> <li>Navigate to the Code Pipeline service in AWS Console and click <strong>Create pipeline</strong>. Give this pipeline a name and leave the rest of the settings on the first page default. We will use v2 pipeline and will let AWS create a service role for Code Pipeline automatically. Remember, service roles control “management plane” access between AWS services. This pipeline will need to be able to access Elastic Beanstalk/EC2. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltd4bdacbf906cd773/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-18.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>On the <strong>Add source stage</strong> page, for <strong>Source provider</strong>, let’s choose <strong>GitHub (Version 2)</strong>. Even though the repository we are using is public, we must use a GitHub account here. Click Connect to GitHub. A new window will pop up. We will set up a GitHub connection here. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt793365cad7441d08/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-19.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>In the pop-up window, type in a name for the <strong>GitHub connection</strong> and click Connect to GitHub. Then click Install a new app and follow the steps to install the <strong>AWS Connector for GitHub</strong> app into your GitHub account. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt38ee93a6082077bc/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-20.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."> You can authorize the app to access all or selected repositories. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blta78533d19774944e/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-22.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."> As I do not plan to use this connection for other projects, I will select only the <strong>smartsheet-webex</strong> repo. After clicking Save, the GitHub App will show in the drop-down, and we will finally be able to click <strong>Connect</strong> to finish this step. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltd03b64e53c1e3531/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-24.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Yay, now the GitHub connection is established, and we can select the repo in the <strong>Code Pipeline</strong> configuration, as well as the <strong>Branch name</strong>. For <strong>Output artifact format</strong>, select <strong>Code Pipeline Default</strong>. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt6fee0322cca12673/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-26.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>The next step is the build stage. Don’t worry, there is nothing to do here for the Python code. It does not require any compilation, build, or artifact generation. Just click <strong>Skip build stage</strong>.</li> <li>On the <strong>Add deploy stage</strong>, select AWS Elastic Beanstalk as the Deploy provider, and select the correct application name and the environment name. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt137e8f4c79619913/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-27.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>The next page is just Review and confirm by clicking the <strong>Create pipeline</strong> button. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt742ee0bc4297556c/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-28.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Elastic Beanstalk will report that the pipeline was successfully created and start executing the pipeline. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltf7b4696954546c0c/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-29.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>After a short while, we can see that the Source stage has completed successfully, and the source code was pulled from GitHub. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt9505b62db1305933/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-30.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>After a couple additional minutes, the Deploy stage should also complete successfully. Our application is now deployed. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt1c0009642a73425c/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-31.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>But is the code running already? Let’s check this by looking into the logs. We can retrieve the logs from the <strong>Logs tab</strong> of the environment page. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltf3282d2f24037b17/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-32.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> </ol> <p>While looking through the log file, under the <code>/var/log/web.stdout.log</code> caption, we can see the following. Is it a good sign? Actually, yes! It shows that Elastic Beanstalk is continuously trying to launch our application, it starts, spits out an error message, and stops. The error generated is a custom message that shows that we haven’t configured the environment variables yet.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt9b04e7557e8faacc/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-33.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <p>But before fixing this, I want to note two important parts of the code package that weren’t visible but made the deployment smooth: <code>.ebextensions</code> and <code>requirements.txt</code>.</p> <h6>What is requirements.txt</h6><p>Almost any Python application is built using external modules. In the local development environment, you typically use package manager <em>pip</em> to install them in your system (or virtual env), and then import them in your code. You end up depending on these modules to make your code work. That’s why the external modules are also called <strong>dependencies</strong>.</p> <p>Elastic Beanstalk wants to create a comfortable environment for your code and supply all the dependencies it needs. But how does it know what Python packages to install for your application? The answer is requirements.txt. This file has the list of dependencies with a specific version for each package. Elastic Beanstalk runs pip that reads this file and installs all the listed Python packages into the environment.</p> <p>Note the last line in the requirements.txt for this project is not like the others. This is because this module – Webex Python SDK – does not have its latest version published in the central Python module repository (PyPI). This line instructs pip to install this module directly from the GitHub repo by running some git commands. But is git even installed in the system?</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt0fd443f04c119fd4/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-34.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <h6>What is .ebextensions</h6><p>The <code>.ebextensions</code> is a folder that was added to the project specifically for Elastic Beanstalk. It has information on additional accommodations Elastic Beanstalk should make for this application. The folder contains multiple files that are processed in order.</p> <p>Let’s look at the first file, <code>00-packages.config</code>. It instructs Elastic Beanstalk to install one additional OS-level package to the EC2 instance – git. Remember why we need git? Of course, to be able to install the Webex SDK dependency directly from GitHub.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt2807fed18a2d51d8/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-35.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <p>The second file, <code>01-flask.config</code> indicates the entry point for our Flask web application. <code>web:app</code> means the server will look in the file named <code>web.py</code> for the application object named <code>app</code>. Here’s the <a href='https://github.com/zhenyamorozov/smartsheet-webex/blob/0b45ca92165c7ca82a854592905af5104ff16c93/web.py#L75' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>place in the code</a> where this application object is created.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt501298cf58ed950c/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-36.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <p>Now, let’s get back to our application. It is running in the Elastic Beanstalk environment, but it is not yet functional. We still need to configure a few environment variables.</p> <h6>Environment variables</h6><p>The <a href='https://github.com/zhenyamorozov/smartsheet-webex/blob/master/docs/get_started.rst#setting-environment-variables' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>documentation</a> of this Webex integration states that there are few environment variables required:</p> <ul> <li><code>SMARTSHEET_ACCESS_TOKEN</code> - your Smartsheet access token</li> <li><code>WEBEX_INTEGRATION_CLIENT_ID</code> - Webex integration Client ID string</li> <li><code>WEBEX_INTEGRATION_CLIENT_SECRET</code> - Webex integration Client Secret</li> <li><code>WEBEX_BOT_TOKEN</code> - Webex bot access token</li> <li><code>WEBEX_BOT_ROOM_ID</code> - Webex bot room ID. This bot can only be used in one Webex room/space. The space can be a direct or a group space.</li> </ul> <p>These values are normally set on the OS environment level of the virtual server. As we are using Elastic Beanstalk, we ideally should not touch the actual EC2 instance at all. We can configure all these variables in the Elastic Beanstalk environment.</p> <ol> <li>Go to the environment home page and click <strong>Configuration</strong> on the left. Scroll all the way down. In the <strong>Environment properties</strong> section, we see that one variable is already set. It is <code>PYTHONPATH</code>. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt5c3f3ee2b04a2a27/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-37.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Let’s add more variables to this list. Click <strong>Edit</strong> on this section, scroll down, and add variables and values one by one. The steps on where to get all these credentials are listed in <a href='https://github.com/zhenyamorozov/smartsheet-webex/blob/master/docs/get_started.rst' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Get Started</a>. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blte5923c223b47a427/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-38.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Note what happens after you click <strong>Apply</strong>. Elastic Beanstalk will take a minute and then report that the new configuration has been deployed on the instance. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt20e263b771ded011/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-39.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Let’s check the log file again. Notice that it stopped yelling at us for the missing environment variable and started the web service successfully. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltdb2e43cb7261f752/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-40.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>And if we open the environment domain name, we can see a response. It means the application is working, available on the public internet, and is ready to receive webhook requests from Webex. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltd9496df27009e34e/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-41.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> </ol> <p>We are almost done, but there will be one more problem to solve. Anyway, let’s see if our bot is working. And it is.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blte9d46d7f0b106639/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-42.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <p>The <strong>Set Smartsheet</strong> and <strong>Authorize Webex</strong> buttons show that there isn’t currently a working smartsheet set, and the Webex integration part of the app does not have any authorization. But before continuing with setting these, we need to tweak something in our AWS setup. The problem is the parameters that are set via the Webex bot are stored securely using yet another AWS service – <strong>Parameter Store</strong>. Parameter Store is part of the AWS SSM (Systems Manager) and can securely store sensitive parameters, such as passwords, keys, and other credentials.</p> <h6>Setting up the Parameter Store</h6><p>We do not have much to do with the Parameter Store itself, but we need to make sure our application has access to it. Yes, it is again about my favorite roles and permissions: they control access between services in AWS.</p> <ol> <li>Let’s go to the IAM service and select Policies. This is the list of AWS-managed policies. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt7256da4897859c62/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-43.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>We will create a <strong>new custom policy</strong> that will allow access to Parameter Store. Click <strong>Create policy</strong>. Select the <strong>Systems Manager</strong> service from the drop-down. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltc7254d30e9fe9f4b/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-44.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Check boxes to enable the actions needed to read and write Parameter Store parameters. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blte2d71b59b359e70f/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-45.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Then, review and save the policy. Next, we need to <em>attach this newly created policy</em> to the role EC2 uses – the instance profile. Select <strong>Roles</strong> on the left and search for the instance profile role. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt9219220afa761ba8/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-46.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Click <strong>Add permissions</strong>, then <strong>Attach policies</strong>, and find our custom policy. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltc880feba11081781/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-47.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> <li>Confirm and verify that the policy has been attached to the instance profile role. <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt772ace429239dc42/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-48.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></li> </ol> <p>And finally, we are all done. We can now set the working smartsheet and authorize the Webex integration via the Webex bot.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltb1cdcce6066e8e2b/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-49.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."> </p> <p>We can even check the stored parameters directly from the AWS Console. Go to the Systems Manager service, then Parameter Store. This application stores two parameters: <strong>Smartsheet ID</strong> and <strong>Webex authentication tokens</strong>.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt9d0d9a57ae205ac9/practical-guide-to-hosting-a-webex-integration-on-aws-51.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <h6>Conclusion</h6><p>Congrats, we finally were able to deploy an actual Webex integration on AWS. Deploying an even moderately complex application on the AWS public cloud can be a daunting task and requires understanding of multiple cloud services. I hope this write-up is not only useful as practical guidance but helps to demonstrate that there is a lot more to cloud deployment than just clicking “launch” when your code is ready to go. For additional support, you can rely on AWS documentation and the <a href='https://community.cisco.com/t5/webex-for-developers/bd-p/disc-webex-developers' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Cisco Webex Developer Community</a>.</p> ]]>
...
</description>

<item>
<title>
<![CDATA[ Webex for Developers Newsletter – February 2024 ]]>
...
</title>
<description>
<![CDATA[ <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt763a01e711986781/61f8604bd970ea1bb42acf6f/Picture1.jpg?width=900&height=317&fit=crop" alt="Webex for Developers Newsletter – February 2024" /> <p>Greetings, Webex Developers! Since the beginning of the year, we have released several new updates that we want to share with you here. Let’s jump right to the details and get caught up on all the news.</p> <h6>📞Introducing the Webex Web Calling SDK</h6><p>We are thrilled to unveil our new <a href='https://github.com/webex/webex-js-sdk/wiki/Introducing-the-Webex-Web-Calling-SDK' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Web Calling SDK</a>, a robust toolkit designed for developers looking to integrate seamless Webex Calling features into their web applications. In a <a data-type='internal' to='/blog/introducing-the-webex-web-calling-sdk'>new blog post</a>, Webex Engineering Leader, Sreekanth Narayanan, highlights all the key SDK features, benefits, and potential integration use cases of this SDK.</p> <h6>🤖Revolutionizing Incident Management in Webex with Command Bots</h6><p>In a <a data-type='internal' to='/blog/revolutionizing-incident-management-with-incident-command-bots'>white paper blog</a> by Webex Developer Relations leader, Luz Delgado-Macias, discover how to optimize incident management with a custom-built Incident Command Bot. Also, learn more about the benefits of automation, power of customization, and unlimited potential for integrating with the Webex platform.</p> <h6>⚙️New Developer How-to Blogs</h6><p>We recently published some helpful new developer blogs that show us how to work with <em>three</em> different types of Webex applications:</p> <h6>Webex Contact Center: Creating a Header Widgets in the Agent Desktop</h6><p>In the first one, the leader of the Webex Developer Evangelism team, Adam Weeks, takes us through a step-by-step lab to <a data-type='internal' to='/blog/developing-with-webex-contact-center-header-widgets-an-rss-feed-reader-example'>create an RSS Feed Reader in a Webex Contact Center Header Widget</a>.</p> <h6>Leveraging Service Apps for Secure and Scalable API Calls</h6><p>Secondly, Webex Developer Evangelist, Joe Zanini, authored a guide to <a data-type='internal' to='/blog/leveraging-service-apps-for-secure-and-scalable-api-calls-a-guide-for-admins-and-developers'>create and manage Webex Service apps</a>, to streamline authorizing org-level integrations for admins, and enabling efficient token consumption for developers to make API calls at scale.</p> <h6>Yarn Workspaces – Mono Repo and the Calling SDK</h6><p>Finally, Webex Engineer, Kesava Krishnan Madavan, explains in detail how we can streamline the development process in the <a data-type='internal' to='/blog/yarn-workspaces-mono-repo-and-the-calling-sdk'>Webex Calling SDK with Yarn Workspaces</a>. Kesava also shows us how these Yarn Workspace strategies can also be applied to various other Webex integration types.</p> <h6>📺Live Webinar: Intro to Webex Connect CPaaS APIs</h6><p>On <strong>Wednesday, February 28th at 1:00PM EST</strong>, join us for the inaugural session of the <a href='https://cpaas.webex.com/' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex Connect</a> webinar series and explore the potential of CPaaS. This session offers a comprehensive introduction to the platform, showcasing the APIs, developer tools and building blocks you can use to integrate powerful communications capabilities into your applications and accelerate customer experience transformation. Learn from a live demonstration how to quickly create and launch customer journeys leveraging serverless computing and AI in a secure and scalable environment. <a href='https://evangelism.webex.com/weblink/register/racd916f80e2689acfa2110e7f4f5bd63' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Register</a> to attend the live webinar or watch the recording after on the <a data-type='internal' to='/webinars'>Developer Webinars page</a>.</p> <h6>🧑‍💻New Developer Guides for Webex Wholesale &amp; Webex for BroadWorks APIs</h6><p>We also just released refreshed developer guides pertaining to <a href='https://help.webex.com/en-us/article/nkguodc/Wholesale-Route-to-Market-Solution-Guide' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex Wholesale</a> and <a href='https://help.webex.com/en-us/article/no4dlj3/Webex-for-Cisco-BroadWorks-Solution-Guide' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex for BroadWorks</a> APIs:</p> <p><a data-type='internal' to='/docs/api/guides/webex-for-wholesale'>Webex for Wholesale Developer Guide</a><strong>:</strong> Learn how to leverage the Webex for Wholesale Provisioning APIs, for allowing Partners to use the Webex Suite as a Package based Utility Model.</p> <p><a data-type='internal' to='/docs/api/guides/webex-for-broadworks-developers-guide'>Webex for BroadWorks Developer Guide</a>: Learn how Service Providers can leverage the Webex for BroadWorks Provisioning APIs, to automatically onboard, update, and remove Webex services for their subscribers.</p> <h6>🦾Embracing the Power of AI at Cisco Live Amsterdam</h6><p>In a <a href='https://blog.webex.com/hybrid-work/webex-integration-partners-cisco-live-amsterdam/?utm_medium=Organic_Social&amp;utm_source=LinkedIn&amp;team=Social' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>post-event wrap up</a>, Business Development Manager, Colm Mcnelis highlights the latest technology innovations that were showcased by our Webex partners, with a special focus on driving digital transformation using the power of AI.</p> <h6>🌅Retiring the Legacy Webex Meetings XML APIs</h6><p>The <a href='https://developer.cisco.com/docs/webex-xml-api-reference-guide/#!meetings-xml-api-reference-guide/webex-meetings-xml-api-reference-guide' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Meetings-related XML APIs</a> have been deprecated and the End-of-Support (EoS) date is planned for the second half of 2023. Cisco will continue to resolve bugs up to this date, but new features will only be implemented for the REST APIs suite. The End-of-life (EoL) timeframe for Meetings-related XML APIs is targeted for <strong>March 31, 2024</strong>, at which time they will be retired. For information on how to migrate from XML to REST APIs, please see the <a href='https://developer.cisco.com/docs/webex-xml-api-reference-guide/#!meetings-xml-api-reference-guide/webex-meetings-xml-api-reference-guide' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex Meetings XML to REST Migration Guide</a>.</p> <h6>📝Webex API Changelog Highlights</h6><p>The <a data-type='internal' to='/docs/api/changelog'>Webex API Changelog</a> has several recent entries listed. We always recommend checking that page frequently to stay up to date. Here are some important entries to note:</p> <ul> <li><strong>February 7, 2024 - BREAKING CHANGE:</strong> If a BroadWorks Subscriber exists but contains errors, the <a data-type='internal' to='/docs/api/v1/broadworks-subscribers/get-a-broadworks-subscriber'>Get a BroadWorks Subscriber</a> and <a data-type='internal' to='/docs/api/v1/broadworks-subscribers/list-broadworks-subscribers'>List BroadWorks Subscribers</a> APIs now return the <code>errorCode</code> as integer in the errors array.</li> <li><strong>January 31, 2024 - NEW:</strong> We are proud to announce the availability of the new <a data-type='internal' to='/docs/api/v1/guests-management'>guest creation mechanism</a> via Service Apps. Guests are now created from authorized Service Apps with guest-issuer scopes</li> <li><strong>January 25, 2024 - NEW</strong>: In the <a data-type='internal' to='/docs/api/v1/virtual-line-call-settings'>Virtual Line Call Settings</a> API, we&#39;ve added multiple endpoints that let you create and manage Virtual Lines and subsets of their call settings.</li> </ul> ]]>

<title>
<![CDATA[ Cisco Live Amsterdam: A Celebration of Innovation and Community ]]>
...
</title>
<description>
<![CDATA[ <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt3c20850783d01f42/65dcc117330e0008d67f57d7/cisco-live-amsterdam-wrap-up-2024-1.png?width=900&height=317&fit=crop" alt="Cisco Live Amsterdam: A Celebration of Innovation and Community" /> <p>As the curtains close on an exhilarating week at Cisco Live Amsterdam, we&#39;re filled with gratitude and inspired by the passion of the global tech community that came together to shape the future of collaboration. From groundbreaking sessions to unforgettable experiences, here&#39;s a recap of the highlights and key takeaways from the event.</p> <h6>Innovative Sessions and Workshops</h6><p>Our Webex developer sessions were a resounding success, with packed rooms and enthusiastic participation. Attendees gained valuable insights into building hybrid experiences, navigating Webex Calling APIs, mastering OAuth 2.0 authorization, and developing for Webex Contact Center. The hands-on workshops ignited creativity, guiding developers through the process of creating embedded apps, building Webex bots, and crafting agent desktop widgets.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt330d5d9e326188d4/cisco-live-amsterdam-wrap-up-2024-2.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <h6>Engagement at the Webex Booths</h6><p>The Webex for Developers Booth in the DevNet Zone buzzed with activity as attendees experienced live demos and connected with our team. Over in the World of Solutions, the Webex and Webex Integration Partners Booths showcased the breadth of possibilities with our platform, highlighting innovative partner-built solutions.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt62d472001366f7de/cisco-live-amsterdam-wrap-up-2024-3.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <h6>Looking Forward</h6><p>As we reflect on the success of Cisco Live Amsterdam, we&#39;re already looking ahead to future events. We&#39;re excited to continue the conversations that started here and to see how the ideas exchanged will evolve into the innovations of tomorrow.</p> <p><img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt2c858937138291f4/cisco-live-amsterdam-wrap-up-2024-4.png" alt="Image described in surrounding text."></p> <p>Thank you to everyone who joined us at Cisco Live Amsterdam. Your energy and curiosity are what make these events so special. Keep the conversation going using #CiscoLiveEMEA and stay tuned for more updates from the Webex team.</p> ]]>

<item>
<title>
<![CDATA[ Introducing SCIM2.0: Revolutionizing User Identity Management on Webex ]]>
...
</title>
<description>
<![CDATA[ <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt1726b917db0d330e/65b93f6241400ce0fd458d7f/scim-2.0-blog-1.png?width=900&height=317&fit=crop" alt="Introducing SCIM2.0: Revolutionizing User Identity Management on Webex" /> <p>We’re excited to announce a groundbreaking update from the Webex Developers team. We&#39;ve been working diligently behind the scenes and are thrilled to unveil our newest feature for user identity management – SCIM2.0.</p> <p>SCIM2.0, or System for Cross-domain Identity Management version 2, is an industry-standard protocol for automating the exchange of user identity information. It&#39;s designed to simplify user management and reduce manual efforts, ensuring a seamless integration process for all developers.</p> <div><Callout type="info">Webex implements SCIM 2.0 as specified in the RFC documents from the Internet Engineering Task Force: </Callout></div> <ul> <li><a href='https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7642' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Definitions, Overview, Concepts, and Requirements: RFC 7642</a></li> <li><a href='https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7643' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Core Schema: RFC 7643</a></li> <li><a href='https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7644' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Protocol: RFC 7644</a></li> </ul> <br/> <h6>Benefits</h6><p>Our new feature will provide a range of benefits including:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Streamlined Identity Management</strong>: With SCIM2.0, managing user identities across various domains becomes a breeze. This feature ensures that user identity information is consistent, efficient, and easy to manage across your applications.</li> <li><strong>Automated User Provisioning</strong>: SCIM2.0 eliminates the need for manual user provisioning. It makes it possible to automate the process of creating, updating, and deactivating user identities in your applications.</li> <li><strong>Improved Efficiency and Productivity</strong>: The automation capabilities of SCIM2.0 reduce manual efforts and errors, thereby increasing efficiency and productivity in your development process.</li> </ul> <p>We believe that this new feature will significantly enhance your user management experience on Webex, making it more efficient and error-free. We&#39;re excited to see how you leverage this feature to improve your applications and services.</p> <p>Our comprehensive documentation on SCIM2.0 will guide you through the process of implementing this new feature into your applications. You can find it at <a data-type='internal' to='/docs/scim-2-overview'>https://developer.webex.com/docs/scim-2-overview</a>.</p> <p>We&#39;re committed to providing you with the tools and features you need to create the best applications possible. With the introduction of SCIM2.0, we&#39;re moving one step closer to that goal.</p> <p>As always, we welcome your feedback and look forward to seeing the innovative ways you&#39;ll use SCIM2. Let&#39;s continue pushing the boundaries of what&#39;s possible in the world of development!</p> <p>Thank you for being a part of the Webex Developer community. Stay tuned for more exciting updates!</p> <h6>Need Some Help? We Got You Covered!</h6><p>We are excited to provide you with support for these features. If you need help, the <a data-type='internal' to='/support'>Webex Developer Support Team</a> is standing by and happy to assist. You can also start or join a conversation on the <a href='https://cs.co/WebexDeveloperCommunity' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex for Developers Community Forum</a>.</p> ]]>
...
</description>

<item>
<title>
<![CDATA[ Introducing the Webex Web Calling SDK ]]>
...
</title>
<description>
<![CDATA[ <img src="https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt8e256ed20b680a19/65b0364014eace52e4a5c7e6/web-calling-sdk-1.png?width=900&height=317&fit=crop" alt="Introducing the Webex Web Calling SDK" /> <p>The Webex Developer Platform team is thrilled to unveil our Web Calling SDK, a new toolkit designed specifically for developers looking to integrate seamless calling features into their web applications using Webex. This SDK is a significant leap forward in our commitment to supplying robust, developer-friendly tools that enhance communication capabilities by now adding Calling workflows in addition to the existing Meetings and Messaging workflows. Whether you&#39;re building a sophisticated enterprise solution or a bespoke web application, our Web Calling SDK offers unparalleled flexibility, ease of use, and the high-quality performance that Webex is renowned for. This makes the Webex JS SDK repository a hub for major workflows available in the <a href='https://www.webex.com/suite/collaboration-suite.html' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex Collaboration Suite</a> (Calling, Meetings and Messaging).</p> <p>In this post, we&#39;ll dive into the key features, benefits, and potential applications of this SDK, giving you all the information you need to start integrating state-of-the-art calling functionality into your web projects.</p> <h6>Journey towards a Web Calling SDK</h6><p>Over the last few years, the Webex application on desktop, mobile (Android &amp; iOS) and Cisco devices supplied access to the calling capabilities of the Webex cloud. However, there were a few challenges here:</p> <ol> <li>It required developers to cross-launch Webex to direct their users from their own applications when a user had to place or answer calls. Users needed to manually navigate back to the original applications during or when the call was completed. This led to a disconnected experience where a user’s attention moved away from their main application.</li> <li>Users were tied to a particular platform. Developers had to add extra logic to support every platform such as Android, iOS, Windows, and Mac.</li> <li>Linux and Chromebooks weren’t supported for the calling workflows.</li> </ol> <p>Thus came the idea of supplying a toolkit for developers where they’d be able to integrate the world-class calling experience right into their applications. We chose the Web platform and WebRTC due to the ubiquitous availability of the underlying technologies.</p> <h6>Building the SDK</h6><p>This SDK is now publicly available as part of the <a href='https://github.com/webex/webex-js-sdk' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex JS SDK mono-repo</a> in GitHub. We added the <a href='https://github.com/webex/webex-js-sdk/tree/next/packages/calling' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>@webex/calling</a> package to the mono-repo as it is familiar to existing developers. The calling package also depends on some of the plugins available in the Webex JS SDK. This made it a logical step to place it within the same repository.</p> <h6>Key Features</h6><p>The Web Calling SDK supplies a robust set of calling features to a developer and user. These features include:</p> <ul> <li>User and device registration with Webex Calling</li> <li>Making and receiving audio calls</li> <li>Hold, Resume and Transfer operations on established calls</li> <li>Switching background noise reduction on and off</li> <li>Mid-call device updates</li> <li>Retrieving call history for a user</li> <li>Retrieve voicemails and marking them read or unread</li> <li>Call quality metrics per call available on-demand (Chromium-based browsers)</li> <li>Managing user’s call preferences</li> </ul> <p>A developer can build a full-fledged calling experience for their users within their existing applications by using the above features exposed in the Web Calling SDK.</p> <h6>Real-World Applications</h6><p>The Web Calling SDK can be used by developers across a multitude of verticals and use-cases. Some of the relevant deployment sweet spots we have seen during the extensive beta phase, include:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Telehealth</strong> – Web applications that allow patients to login and place calls to their respective physician. Conversely, a portal for physicians where they can place to and receive calls from patients, consultants, and partners.</li> <li><strong>Finance</strong> – The Calling SDK can be imported into applications and devices used for trades by stockbrokers to supply calling capabilities within the workspace&#39;s context.</li> <li><strong>CRM applications</strong> – These applications can use calling capabilities for agents to place and receive calls within the application itself, allowing them to aid their customers quickly and efficiently. For instance, Webex for Salesforce is currently changing to consume this SDK.</li> </ul> <br/> <h6>Productized Apps that use the Calling SDK</h6><br/> <ul> <li>The <a href='https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/webex-calling-for-chrome/llllflgakifpdcmoanonghipldcpaggn?pli=1' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex Calling for Chrome</a> extension leverages the Web Calling SDK to provide its capabilities. </li> <li>Another consumer of the SDK is <a href='https://help.webex.com/en-us/article/ngmx08cb/Webex-Calling-for-Microsoft-Teams' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex Calling for MS Teams</a>.</li> </ul> <br/> <h6>Integrating the Web Calling SDK into your projects</h6><p>To get started, visit the <a data-type='internal' to='/docs/sdks/webex-calling-sdk'>Webex Calling SDK</a> page in the Webex Developer Portal. This will redirect you to the <a href='https://github.com/webex/webex-js-sdk/wiki/Quickstart-Guide-(Calling)' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>QuickStart Guide</a> where you can find code snippets to begin importing and experimenting with the SDK.</p> <p>You will need to have Webex Calling licenses to start integrating these flows into your application. Using a developer sandbox is a good way to start.</p> <h6>Best Practices</h6><p>Some things to familiarize yourself with before using the SDK:</p> <ul> <li>OAuth flows used to <a data-type='internal' to='/docs/integrations'>Authenticate with Webex</a>. This provides an access token with privileges to interact with the Webex cloud for services like calling, messaging, and meetings.</li> <li><a href='https://webex.github.io/webex-js-sdk/samples/calling/' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Kitchen sink page for Calling SDK</a> – This sample application allows you to evaluate the various features exposed by the Web Calling SDK.</li> <li><a href='https://github.com/WebexSamples/web-calling-sdk-samples' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Sample applications</a> that consume the Calling SDK</li> </ul> <br/> <h6>Looking Ahead</h6><p>Exciting features are planned for future updates of the Web Calling SDK. Among these are</p> <ul> <li>Calling for guest users</li> <li>Video calls</li> <li>Calling widgets</li> </ul> <br/> <h6>Get Started Now</h6><p>The Web Calling SDK, with its versatile and robust capabilities across various industries, from healthcare and education to finance and customer service is ready to take the industry to new heights. Its flexible integration and expansive feature set opens endless possibilities for developers to innovate and tailor solutions to the unique demands and workflows of different sectors.</p> <h6>Need Some Help? We Got You Covered!</h6><p>We are excited to provide you with support for these features. If you need help, the <a data-type='internal' to='/support'>Webex Developer Support Team</a> is standing by and happy to assist. You can also start or join a conversation on the <a href='https://cs.co/WebexDeveloperCommunity' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Webex for Developers Community Forum</a>. Additionally, the <a href='https://github.com/webex/webex-js-sdk/issues' rel='noopener noreferrer' target='_blank'>Issues</a> page for our repository is the place to come to if you’re looking to give us some feedback.</p> ]]>

# Meet webex-node: The Webex JavaScript SDK Built for Node.js
July 10, 2026
![Adam Weeks](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt3280371eceea2196/6a60ed759ee77e32d96ed610/Adam_Headshot_Cropped.png?width=100&height=100&fit=crop)
Adam WeeksTechnical Leader, Webex Developer Relations
![Meet webex-node: The Webex JavaScript SDK Built for Node.js](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt55273c6aaa9c88f5/6a51535730ac2679a93fa148/webex-node-sdk-blog-header.png?width=900&height=317&fit=crop)
The [`webex-node`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/webex-node) package gives server-side JavaScript a supported Webex SDK entry point for Messaging, automation, bots, command-line tools, and backend services without loading browser-only media components.
* * *
## Why a Node.js-Specific Package?
For years, the [`webex`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/webex) npm package has given JavaScript developers a convenient way to add Webex capabilities to an application. It remains the right choice for browser experiences—including applications that use Webex Meetings, Calling, or Contact Center.
But a browser and a Node.js process are very different environments. A browser supplies APIs such as `window` and the media stack needed for real-time audio and video. A command-line script, automation worker, or backend service does not. Beginning with version 3 of the SDK, importing the full `webex` package directly into Node.js could load browser-dependent media components and fail with a `window is not defined` error.
That is the gap [`webex-node`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/webex-node) was created to fill.
Released in April 2025 and now documented on the [Webex for Developers Node.js SDK page](https://developer.webex.com/messaging/docs/sdks/node), `webex-node` provides a supported Webex JavaScript SDK entry point designed specifically for a Node.js runtime. It preserves the familiar SDK programming model for Messaging and related Webex APIs while leaving out browser-only media components.
## One SDK Family, Two Runtime-Focused Packages
Both packages come from the same [`webex-js-sdk`](https://github.com/webex/webex-js-sdk) project and share the same core concepts. In either environment, developers initialize a Webex client and work with APIs such as rooms, messages, memberships, people, teams, and webhooks.
The important difference is what each package loads and where it is intended to run.  
| Choose  | When your application runs in  | Best suited for  |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| `webex-node`  | Node.js, without a browser DOM  | CLI tools, scheduled jobs, automation, bots, webhook services, and backend integrations using Messaging and related REST-backed APIs  |  
| `webex`  | A web browser or browser-bundled application  | Interactive web experiences, especially those using Meetings, Calling, Contact Center, or other browser media capabilities  |  
The full `webex` package includes media-oriented dependencies for Meetings, Calling, and Contact Center. Those capabilities rely on browser facilities and are intentionally excluded from `webex-node`. The result is not a second, unrelated SDK. It is a Node-focused distribution of the same SDK family with a runtime-appropriate capability boundary.
That boundary is also the principal limitation to remember: `webex-node` cannot be used for Meetings, Calling, or Contact Center media flows. If an application needs to join a meeting, place a call, or handle media in the browser, use `webex` and the appropriate browser SDK documentation.
## What Is webex-node Good For?
The package is a natural fit anywhere Webex work should happen without a visible browser interface.
### Command-Line Utilities
A developer can build a terminal command that creates a project space, posts release notes, looks up a person, or adds members to a space. This is useful for internal tooling and repeatable operational workflows where opening a web page would only add friction.
### CI/CD and Scheduled Automation
A Node.js job can post deployment results to a Webex space, create a collaboration space for a new project, or send a daily report. The same approach works in a CI pipeline, a cron job, a container, or a serverless function with a supported Node.js runtime.
### Backend Integrations
An Express, Fastify, or other Node.js service can use `webex-node` to connect application events with Webex. For example, a service could receive a business event, format a notification, and post it to the appropriate space. It can also create and manage Webex webhooks as part of an integration.
### Messaging Bots and Workflow Services
For a bot or workflow that needs direct SDK access, `webex-node` provides the underlying Messaging APIs without pulling browser media modules into the process. A production bot will still need an inbound-event design—typically Webex webhooks delivered to a publicly reachable endpoint—but its outbound Webex operations can use the SDK's rooms, messages, memberships, and related APIs.
### Administrative and Migration Scripts
One-off scripts are often the fastest way to perform a controlled bulk task: inspect spaces, reconcile memberships, or move a repeatable API procedure into source control. `webex-node` lets Node.js developers do that through SDK methods instead of assembling every HTTP request by hand.
## A First Node.js Script
The current getting-started guide calls for Node.js 20 and npm 10. Create a project and install the package:

```
mkdir webex-node-hello
cd webex-node-hello
npm init -y
npm install webex-node

```

Add `"type": "module"` to `package.json`, then create `index.js`:

```
import WebexNode from 'webex-node';

const webex = WebexNode.init({
  credentials: {
    access_token: process.env.WEBEX_ACCESS_TOKEN,
  },
});

webex.once('ready', async () => {
  try {
    if (!webex.canAuthorize) {
      throw new Error('Webex authorization failed');
    }

    const room = await webex.rooms.create({
      title: 'Hello from Node.js',
    });

    await webex.messages.create({
      roomId: room.id,
      markdown: '**Hello from `webex-node`!**',
    });

    console.log(`Created space: ${room.title}`);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  }
});

```

Set a token in the environment and run the script:

```
WEBEX_ACCESS_TOKEN='<your-token>' node index.js

```

For a quick local test, a personal access token can help validate the flow. Personal access tokens are short-lived and intended for development only. For a production workload, use the authentication model appropriate to the application—such as a Webex bot or an OAuth integration—and keep credentials out of source code.
When troubleshooting, the SDK also supports log-level control through the environment. For example:

```
WEBEX_LOG_LEVEL=debug WEBEX_ACCESS_TOKEN='<your-token>' node index.js

```

## How to Choose
The simplest decision rule is to choose by runtime and required capability:
  * If the code runs as a Node.js process and needs Messaging or related management APIs, start with `webex-node`.
  * If the code runs in a browser and needs a user-facing Webex experience, use `webex`.
  * If the application needs Meetings, Calling, or Contact Center media flows, use `webex`; those capabilities are outside the scope of `webex-node`.
  * If the solution has both a browser frontend and a Node.js backend, it can use both packages—each on its own side of the application boundary.


That last pattern is often the most useful. A browser can own the interactive experience and real-time media, while a backend safely performs scheduled work, responds to webhooks, and integrates Webex with other systems.
## A Clearer Path for Server-Side JavaScript
`webex-node` does not introduce a separate set of Webex APIs. Its most important capability is simpler and more practical: it gives server-side JavaScript a supported package boundary that matches the Node.js runtime.
For developers building terminal tools, automation, bots, and backend services, that means no browser shim, no accidental dependency on `window`, and no need to load media capabilities the application will never use. Install the package, initialize the familiar Webex client, and put Webex Messaging to work wherever Node.js runs.
To get started, visit the [Webex Node.js SDK documentation](https://developer.webex.com/messaging/docs/sdks/node) or explore the [`webex-node` source and README](https://github.com/webex/webex-js-sdk/tree/next/packages/webex-node).

# From Waveform to Insight: A Compiler for Customer Intent
May 19, 2026
![Jason Vaccaro & Francis Kurupacheril](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltf1a11d59afde7c75/617175c0da02001d99f29106/cisco-webex-devs-avatar.png?width=100&height=100&fit=crop)
Jason Vaccaro & Francis KurupacherilWebex Contact Center
![From Waveform to Insight: A Compiler for Customer Intent](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blted34b8dfaac80e59/6a172d92a6c2b99fb6e79a26/topic-analytics-generated-blog-header.png?width=900&height=317&fit=crop)
Every contact center sits on the same paradox: the most valuable signal in the business — _why customers are actually calling_ — flows past in a medium (speech) that almost no downstream system can consume. Analytics dashboards speak in joinable rows and columns; conversations arrive as waveforms. The gap between those two representations is where containment strategies die, where staffing plans go stale, and where emerging issues incubate for weeks before anyone notices. 
**Topic Analytics** is how we close that gap. And the useful way to think about it is not as a dashboard or a report, but as a _semantic compiler_ : a multi-stage pipeline that lowers acoustic signal into a typed, clustered, labeled ontology of customer intent — in near real time, on every interaction, at contact-center scale. 
> A compiler takes a language humans write fluently but machines cannot reliably execute — loose, ambiguous, full of context only a reader can resolve — and lowers it, stage by stage, into symbolic instructions a machine can act on. Topic Analytics is the same idea, applied to the language humans speak most fluently of all: conversation. Free-form, discursive, full of digressions and repairs — and, until now, completely opaque to any database downstream of it. The pipeline lowers it into symbols a BI system can join on. 
  

### The problem, stated precisely
Contact center supervisors are under pressure to improve containment (deflect more to self-service), lift agent productivity, and protect CSAT. Each of those levers depends on a single upstream primitive: **a reliable, current distribution of contact reasons**. Without it, you cannot: 
  * Pick the right automation candidates — the topics with the highest volume and lowest variance in intent.
  * Plan staffing and training against _real_ demand rather than last quarter's call codes.
  * Detect emerging issues while they are still faint, before a mis-priced SKU or a broken deployment becomes a CSAT cliff.


The incumbent answer — agent-selected disposition codes plus sampled manual QA — is slow, biased, and low-resolution. It answers "what did an agent remember to click after a call?" not "what is the population of customer intents right now?" 
* * *
  

### Architecture: a seven-stage pipeline
Topic Analytics is engineered as a purpose-built pipeline for contact-center interactions, rather than a general-purpose NLP toolkit bolted onto the side of the platform. Each stage is independently scalable and independently evaluable, and each stage's output is the next stage's typed input. 
![Seven-stage Topic Analytics pipeline](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt55656a1e0f925f40/6a172d941949f7450be7add0/topic-analytics-pipeline-bright.svg)
_**Figure 1.** The pipeline. Stages 1–7 run per-interaction in near real time; stage 6 feeds a slower, continuous retraining loop back into stage 4._
#### Stage 1: Speech-to-Text transcription
Streaming ASR optimized for the phonetic and prosodic characteristics of contact-center audio — narrow-band telephony codecs, accented speakers, background noise, hold music. Because the caller leg and the agent leg are captured and processed as _separate_ audio streams, transcripts are produced with speaker labels directly — no ML diarization model required to untangle who said what. The two streams are stitched back together with clean provenance on every utterance, which matters downstream: distinguishing the customer's words from the agent's is essential when we go looking for the _customer's_ reason for contact.
#### Stage 2: Redaction
Before any transcript touches the LLM, it passes through a PII-aware redactor. Named entities, account numbers, payment credentials, dates of birth, and health data are replaced with typed placeholders (`<CARD_NUMBER>`, `<DOB>`). This is not just a compliance boundary — it is an _information-theoretic_ boundary. Redacting tokens that would otherwise dominate attention weights (long digit spans, proper nouns) forces the extraction model to condition on the actual intent phrases, which improves topic coherence downstream.
#### Stage 3: LLM-powered contact-reason extraction
A purpose-prompted LLM reads the redacted transcript and emits a compact, canonicalized phrase that captures the customer's _reason for contact_ — not a summary, not a sentiment, not an agent action. A flight-status call becomes `"check flight delay status"`; a billing call becomes `"dispute duplicate charge"`. Producing a normalized reason phrase — rather than trying to cluster the full transcript — is what makes the rest of the pipeline tractable.
#### Stage 4: Dynamic clustering
Reason phrases are embedded into a dense vector space. Clusters are discovered _dynamically_ — the number of topics is not fixed in advance — using an **incremental clustering algorithm** that assigns each new point online as it arrives, spawns a new cluster when no existing region is a sufficiently good neighbor, and lets clusters evolve as more data accumulates. Because the algorithm is incremental rather than batch, it is what makes the "near" in near real time possible: we are not re-running a batch clustering algorithm over a historical window on every tick, we are updating the topic space as each interaction lands. (An earlier generation of Topic Analytics was built on a batch clustering algorithm; the NRT system is not.) This is the stage that lets a new product launch or a novel defect manifest as a new topic within hours, not quarters.
#### Stage 5: Automatic topic labeling
Each cluster is named by a second LLM pass that reads a sample of its member phrases and produces a 2–3 word human-readable label (`Flight status`, `Refund request`, `Baggage help`). Labels are constrained to be noun-phrase-shaped and terminology-aware — the model has context about the customer's industry so it favors _domain_ language over _generic_ language.
#### Stage 6: User-centric topic customization
AI-generated topics are a starting point, not an endpoint. Admins can seed pre-defined topics at configuration time (typed in, or uploaded as CSV/XLSX), rename AI-generated labels, and merge clusters that the model split too finely. Those human edits are first-class signals: they flow back into the clustering stage as soft constraints on the next run. This is the difference between "the AI is wrong, retrain it" and "the AI learned what _your_ business calls that thing."
#### Stage 7: Continuous insights
The final stage is the one that makes the rest useful: emitting topic assignments as typed fields on every interaction, available in the Analyzer dashboard and over the API as custom report columns (`Topic Name`, `Contact Driver`). This is where the pipeline re-enters the BI world. You can now `GROUP BY topic` and ask the real questions: which topics have the worst CSAT? the longest AHT? the steepest week-over-week growth?
> **The loop is the product.** A one-shot topic model decays the moment the business changes. Topic Analytics is explicitly designed as a closed loop: human curation in stage 6 becomes training signal for stage 4, which changes the labels stage 5 generates, which surfaces new topics to curate in stage 6. The dashboards are the _readout_ of a system that is always learning the shape of _your_ demand.
* * *
  

### A seismograph, not a thermometer
The second metaphor that is useful here: Topic Analytics is a _seismograph_ , not a thermometer. A thermometer reports a scalar — call volume is up, CSAT is down — and by the time a thermometer reading becomes alarming, the event has already happened. A seismograph picks up weak signals spatially distributed across a surface and lets you see the tremor _where_ it originated, long before it becomes an earthquake. 
Because every interaction is labeled, not just a sample, the system can detect cluster-level anomalies: a topic that did not exist last week, a topic whose handle time doubled overnight, a topic whose CSAT collapsed on a specific queue. These are the faint tremors — the single-digit percentage shifts in the tail — that predict the headline incident. 
![Topic volume as a seismograph over time](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt2ff2df7e605a7631/6a172d95961e6901a1c4d21e/topic-analytics-seismograph-bright.svg)
_**Figure 2.** Known topics track their baselines; a novel cluster — call it "boarding-pass app error" — appears at week 3 and spikes at week 4. Topic Analytics names and surfaces it _while it is still small_ , not after it tops the volume chart._
* * *
  

### Why the embedding space shape matters
The design choice that carries the most weight is actually stage 4: _incremental, online_ clustering on extracted reason phrases, rather than classification into a fixed taxonomy. The implication is worth stating plainly. 
A fixed-taxonomy classifier is a decision about the world frozen at training time. When a new SKU launches, when a regulatory change creates a new category of call, when two previously distinct topics merge because the business process unified — a classifier cannot tell you, because it does not have a label for the thing it is seeing. It will quietly bucket the new calls into the nearest existing class, and the dashboard will continue to look normal. 
Incremental online clustering is the opposite. Each new reason phrase is compared against the current cluster structure as it arrives; points that are not a sufficiently good fit for any existing region are _allowed to remain unassigned_ until enough of them accumulate to form their own. When that region crosses the threshold, a new cluster is born, stage 5 names it, and it starts producing dashboard readings — without any offline retraining step. The system's ontology tracks the business's ontology, on its own. 
![Embedding space before and after a new topic emerges](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt20d41cb5703af29d/6a172d96b339d5066276a319/topic-analytics-embedding-space-bright.svg)
_**Figure 3.** The same embedding space, three weeks apart. A new high-density region crosses the cluster-birth threshold and gets named automatically. A fixed-taxonomy system would have silently buried these calls in "Other."_
* * *
  

### What this looks like at the edge — the surface area
Inside the product, the compiler's output shows up in three surfaces: 
  

### 1. The Topic Analytics dashboard
The primary UI — the one that ops leaders live in — is organized around the questions the pipeline was built to answer. Highest interaction volume. Longest average handle time. Highest and lowest CSAT. Top five topics by trend. Trending-topics table with per-topic sample-contact drill-down, filterable by queue and time window, refreshable on demand. This is the readout. 
![Topic Analytics dashboard: volume cards, Top 5 topics trend chart, top topics by CSAT and average handle time, Trending topics table](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/blt4d499a99a7d0e216/6a172d93961e6929efc4d21a/topic-analytics-dashboard.png)
_**Figure 4.** The Topic Analytics dashboard. The entire compiler stack exists to make this view possible — every card and column is a `GROUP BY topic` away from the raw interaction stream._
  

### 2. Topic drill-down
For any single topic you can pivot into _that topic's world_ : its volume curve over time, its channel mix (voice / chat / email / SMS), the full list of associated interactions, and — crucially — the actual transcripts. The compiler can be trusted, but you can always inspect what it compiled. 
![Topic drill-down view for the Flight status topic: performance-over-time chart, interaction-by-channel breakdown, associated-interactions table](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltd74e2c7e18c68b20/bltcac0defeea81a07e/6a172d93c1e8a578f5f885f8/topic-analytics-drilldown.png)
_**Figure 5.** Topic drill-down. Every aggregate statistic is traceable back to the individual conversations that produced it — the compiler's output is always inspectable._
  

### 3. Analyzer + API
Two new custom fields — `Topic Name` and `Contact Driver` — are exposed as first-class columns inside the Analyzer reporting engine and over the public API. The same fields that power the native dashboards are available to your existing reports, your data warehouse, and your BI stack. The output of the pipeline is not a walled garden; it is a join key. 
Copy

```
// Example: join your existing interaction warehouse to Topic Analytics output
SELECT
  t.topic_name,
  COUNT(*)                            AS interactions,
  AVG(i.handle_time_s)              AS avg_aht,
  AVG(i.auto_csat)                  AS avg_csat,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE i.contained) AS deflected
FROM   interactions i
JOIN   topic_analytics t USING (interaction_id)
WHERE  i.created_at >= '2026-04-01'
GROUP BY t.topic_name
ORDER BY interactions DESC;

```

That query — a week of contact-center demand, sliced by intent, with automation and CSAT signal attached — is the one an ops leader could not write at all before, because the `topic_name` column did not exist. The entire pipeline is the machinery required to make one join key meaningful. 
* * *
  

### The engineering problems this actually solves
#### Cold start
A clustering system needs data before it can cluster. Most tenants do not want to run blind while the model learns what their calls are about. Pre-defined topics solve this: admins seed an initial topic list at configuration time (typed or uploaded as a CSV/XLSX), and those names are matched against interactions from day one. AI-generated topics accumulate alongside the pre-defined ones, and the pre-defined list provides anchors that stabilize the embedding space while the long tail is being discovered. 
#### Label drift
LLM-generated labels are a moving target — the same cluster can get named "Refund request" one day and "Request for refund" the next if you are not careful. The system pins labels to cluster identity, not to generation runs, so the same cluster keeps its name across re-runs unless an admin renames it (which then becomes the pinned label, overriding the AI). 
#### Long-tail topics
In a realistic contact center, the distribution is heavy-tailed: the top 20 topics are 80% of volume, and there are thousands of rare intents in the tail. Incremental online clustering is well-suited to this — it will form a cluster for a rare intent once enough related points have arrived, and leave individual oddities unassigned until they find neighbors. The tail remains inspectable without drowning the dashboard. 
#### Cross-language support
The April–June 2026 release extends the pipeline to multi-language voice interactions and to digital channels (chat, email, SMS) — including AI-agent interactions, which close the loop between automation and the analytics that tell you whether the automation is actually working. The architecture accommodates this because every stage from redaction onward operates on text in a language-general way, with only stage 1 (ASR) and the extraction prompt in stage 3 needing to be language-aware. 
* * *
  

### Where this goes next
The roadmap telegraphs the ambition. Shipped in Q1 2026: near real-time discovery and pre-defined topic names. Shipping this quarter: multi-language voice, digital interactions, and AI Agent interactions. On the horizon: **topic-to-AI-agent creation** — the system identifies a high-volume topic with low variance in intent, and offers to generate an AI agent scoped to that topic. Topic themes for hierarchical organization. Topic insights for automated narrative over the trend data. 
That last one — topic-to-agent — is the closing of the biggest loop in the contact center. Today, Topic Analytics tells you which calls are the best candidates for automation. Tomorrow, it builds the automation. The compiler stops describing the program and starts writing it. 
> Every contact center has always had its reasons-for-contact. They were just encoded in a medium — audio — that no dashboard could read. Topic Analytics is the translation layer: it lowers conversation into a joinable fact, and it does so continuously, on every interaction, in the business's own language. The dashboards are downstream. The pipeline is the point. 
* * *
